keywords: Cap / hat / container cap distinction pilleus, pilleī m. pilleus, pilleī m. — close-fitting cap or hat, originally of felt; Traupman uses it for “cap” (pp. 116 and 286). Applied here to modern caps without claiming every modern shape was ancient. Pilleum indue. — Put on your cap. Ubi est pilleus tuus? — Where is your cap? A container’s cap or lid is operculum, operculī n. , not this headwear noun. See the lid / blender entry . The alternative single-l spelling pīleus has a different vowel-quantity convention; this entry follows Traupman’s pilleus . Sources & evidence Lewis & Short: pilleus · Morgan–Owens: hat: cap · Traupman: Conversational Latin, fourth edition

english: Wear / put on / dress up / try on / fits / too tight / too loose / barefoot / warm / light
latin: gerō, gerere, gessī, gestum · nūdīs pedibus
keywords: wear wearing what to wear dressed up dress up decked out try on does it fit fits too tight too small too loose too big shoes pinch barefoot bare feet warm clothes light clothes thin

items.html: gerō, gerere, gessī, gestum; gestō, gestāre — wear (Traupman 118, 405); ūtor, ūtī + abl. — wear regularly (Traupman 405): perspicillīs ūtī, wear glasses. Leda complains habeō nihil prōrsus quod geram — “I have absolutely nothing to wear” (Traupman 114).
sē exōrnāre — dress up (Traupman 116); Quamobrem sīc subōrnātus es? — Why are you all dressed up? (Traupman 96).
induendō probāre — try on (Traupman 118); M-O: experīrī (Egger: velim experīrī haec calceāmenta).

Hī calceī sunt aptī ad pedēs. — These shoes fit (M-O, after Egger; Cic. de Or. 1.231 calceī habilēs et aptī ad pedem). pede majōrēs / minōrēs — too big / too small (M-O); Horace: ut calceus ōlim, sī pede major erit, subvertet, sī minor, ūret — “like a shoe: too big it trips you, too small it pinches” (Ep. 1.10.42–43). Traupman: strīctus (394 strīct·us), tight; laxus, loose; sī calceus ūrit (342, 360, 394).
nūdīs pedibus — barefoot (M-O; Hor. S. 1.8.24; Plin. Ep. 2.17.15 nūdīsque etiam pedibus mollis); discalceātus, discalceāta, discalceātum — unshod (M-O; Suet.).
calidus — warm, of clothes (M-O; Plaut. Mil. 687 pallium … calidum); tenuis — light, thin (M-O; Hor., Ov.).
Quid hodiē gerēs? — What are you going to wear today?
Calceī tibi pede minōrēs sunt; novōs emēmus. — Your shoes are too small; we’ll buy new ones.
Vīsne nūdīs pedibus per herbam currere? — Do you want to run barefoot through the grass?

english: Outdoor wear: hood / raincoat / coat / jacket / gloves / mittens / scarf / hat / umbrella / boots / trainers
latin: cucullus, cucullī m. · digitābula, digitābulōrum n. · fōcāle, fōcālis n.
keywords: hood hooded raincoat rain jacket waterproof coat overcoat jacket windbreaker gloves mittens scarf neck scarf hat sun hat broad-brimmed swim cap shower cap umbrella parasol boots wellies rubber boots trainers sneakers sandals shoelaces

items.html: cucullus, cucullī m. — hood (Juv. 3.170; Mart.; Columella); paenula cucullāta — hooded coat (M-O). Traupman’s ploxenum (216, 329) is the hood of a car, not a garment; classically ploxemum or ploxenum is a Gallic word for a wagon-box (Catull. 97.6, quoted by Quintilian).

paenula, paenulae f. — raincoat, the ancient rain-cloak (Traupman 117 for a hooded one; M-O, citing Varr. ap. Non. paenula in imbrī and Juv. 5.79). scortea, scorteae f. — leather raincoat (Traupman 117; Sen., Mart.). M-O also gives pluviāle (medieval) and, from LRL, paenula impermeābilis (with a query).

amiculum, amiculī n. — coat, mantle (Traupman 116; M-O; Cic.); superindūmentum, superindūmentī n. — overcoat (Traupman 117; M-O; Tertullian, ecclesiastical). jacca, jaccae f. — jacket (Traupman 117, modern; Traupman spells it with i); M-O: tunica (Vives) and, for a windbreaker, tunica levior.

digitābula, digitābulōrum n. — gloves (Traupman 321; Helfer and LRL as cited by the Neo-Latin Lexicon); Varro’s single digitābulum is an olive-picker’s glove (RR 1.55.1). Traupman 116 also gives digitālia, not in L&S. M-O prefers chīrothēca (medieval; see the cycling-gloves entry), distinguishing chīrothēca digitāta, glove, from chīrothēca continua, mitten. Pliny’s scribe kept his hands warm in winter with long sleeves: cujus manūs hieme manicīs mūniēbantur (Ep. 3.5.15).
fōcāle, fōcālis n. — scarf, muffler (M-O; Hor. S. 2.3.255; Mart.; from faucēs); Traupman 117 gives amictōrium, a late word (Cod. Th.).
petasus, petasī m. — broad-brimmed hat, sun hat (Traupman 117; M-O; Plaut.). See the cap entry for pilleus. galērum natātōrium / balneārium — swim cap / shower cap (M-O, modern).
umbella, umbellae f. — umbrella (Traupman 399); classically a parasol (Mart., Juv.), as M-O notes; see the weather entry.
calceī gymnicī — trainers, sneakers (Traupman 118, 381; M-O calceus gymnicus).

pērō, pērōnis m. — rawhide boot (Traupman 116; Verg., Juv.); ocreae, ocreārum f. — boots (M-O, citing Erasmus); classically greaves, leggings. Neither source has rubber boots; calceī altī cummeī would be our formation.
Cucullum indue; pluit. — Put your hood up; it’s raining.
Ubi sunt digitābula tua? — Where are your gloves?
Fōcāle collō circumdā; frīgus est. — Put your scarf round your neck; it’s cold.

english: Clothes II: T-shirt / long-sleeved / sleeveless / shorts / underpants / underwear / tights / swimsuit / bathrobe / dress / skirt / jeans
latin: tunicula, tuniculae f. · subligāculum, subligāculī n. · vestis balneāris
keywords: T-shirt tee shirt long-sleeved short-sleeved sleeveless shorts swimming trunks underpants pants briefs boxers underwear tights pantyhose swimsuit swimming costume bathing suit bathrobe dressing gown housecoat dress skirt jeans denim overalls dungarees apron vest waistcoat

items.html: tunicula, tuniculae f. — T-shirt (Traupman 389; classically a little tunic, Plaut.); M-O: camīsula, camisiola, or camisia levis (modern). For shirts see the shirt entry; M-O’s camisia (Jerome) and indūsium are post-classical in this sense.
manicātus, manicāta, manicātum — long-sleeved (Traupman 117; Cic.); sine manicīs — sleeveless (Traupman 118); dīmidiīs manicīs — short-sleeved (M-O, after Vives).
brācae curtae / dēcurtātae — shorts (Traupman 378; M-O); Traupman’s subligāculum and M-O’s feminālia are underpants or loin-cloths in antiquity.

subligāculum, subligāculī n.; subligar, subligāris n. — underpants, briefs (M-O; Cic. Off. 1.129, a loin-cloth; subligar in Mart. and Juv.). Traupman: brācae interiōrēs (400). vestēs intimae — underwear (M-O); Traupman 400 gives subūcula, which is the undershirt.
crūrālia, crūrālium n. — tights (M-O, from LRL; modern); Helfer’s tībiālia brācāria.
vestis balneāris — swimsuit (Traupman 118); M-O: vestis natātōria. subligar balneāre / natātōrium — swimming trunks (Traupman 118; M-O).
vestis mātūtīna — dressing gown, housecoat (Traupman 117); M-O: amictus domesticus; bathrobe amictus balneāris.

vestis muliebris; stola, stolae f. — dress (Traupman 116; M-O); vestis tālāris — long dress. Skirt: Traupman 118 gives castula and indūcula, both ancient women’s under-garments, and M-O gives Plautus’s calthula; none means a modern skirt, so we leave the word open.
brācae Genuēnsēs — jeans (Traupman 335; M-O, from Helfer).
colobium, colobiī n. — vest, waistcoat (M-O; Servius, late).

Traupman 355 gives encombōma for overalls, but L&S defines it as a white garment worn by girls (Varr.); M-O’s superindūmentum operārium (LRL) is queried. Apron: see the kitchen-tools entry (praecīnctōrium); Traupman 272 subligar, M-O līmus (Verg., a sacrificial apron).
Hodiē calet: tuniculam et brācās curtās indue. — It’s hot today: put on a T-shirt and shorts.
Vestem balneārem et linteum in pēram pōnāmus. — Let’s put your swimsuit and towel in the bag.

english: Jewellery and accessories: necklace / earrings / bracelet / pearl / brooch / pocket / handbag / handkerchief / glasses / wristwatch
latin: monīle, monīlis n. · inaurēs, inaurium f. · armilla, armillae f.
keywords: jewellery jewelry necklace chain earrings bracelet bangle pearl pearls brooch safety pin clasp buckle charm amulet pocket handbag purse wallet handkerchief hanky glasses spectacles eyeglasses watch wristwatch jewellery shop collar cuff

items.html: monīle, monīlis n.; torquis (torquēs), torquis m. — necklace (Traupman 117; Cic. Verr. 2.4.39; Verg. A. 1.654); monīle gemmātum — jewelled necklace (Traupman 115).
inaurēs, inaurium f. — earrings (Traupman 116; Plaut. Men. 3.3.17, in L&S).
armilla, armillae f. — bracelet (Traupman 116; M-O; Plaut., Liv.); M-O also bracchiāle (Plin.).
margarīta, margarītae f. — pearl (Traupman 117; Varr., Cic.).
fībula, fībulae f. — brooch, clasp, safety pin, buckle (Traupman 116, 283, 373; M-O s.v. buckle).
amulētum, amulētī n. — charm, amulet (Traupman 116; Plin.).
loculus, loculī m. — pocket (Traupman 117, 362); M-O: funda vestis (Badellino, Helfer) and sinus (LRL). See the walk entry for sinus, the fold of a coat used as a pocket.
pērula, pērulae f. — handbag, little bag (Traupman 117; M-O; Sen. Ep. 90.14 exemptum ē pērulā calicem); see the dad’s-bag entry for crumēna.

sūdārium, sūdāriī n.; sūdāriolum, sūdāriolī n. — handkerchief (M-O; Mart., Petr., Suet.; the diminutive is Apuleius). Cordier: Dēterge faciem sūdāriolō (Coll. 2.69). See also the blow-your-nose entry.
vitra oculāria — glasses (Traupman 312; LRL and Levine per the Neo-Latin Lexicon); perspicilla, perspicillōrum n. (Traupman; Erasmus, Renaissance). perspicillīs ūtī — wear glasses (Traupman).
hōrologium bracchiāle — wristwatch (Traupman 118, 409 hōrologium armillāre); Neo-Latin Lexicon s.v. watch: hōrologium gestābile (Helfer).
taberna gemmāria — jewellery shop (M-O, after Egger; Traupman 335 gemmāria).
collāre, collāris n. — collar (Traupman 116; M-O, from Comenius); limbus manicae — cuff (M-O).
Quid in loculō habēs? Lapidēs iterum? — What have you got in your pocket? Stones again?
Avia monīle et inaurēs gerit. — Grandma is wearing a necklace and earrings.

english: Fabrics: cotton / linen / wool / silk / leather / felt / fur / cloth
latin: gossypium, gossypiī n. · līnum, līnī n. · lāna, lānae f.
keywords: fabric material cloth cotton linen wool woollen silk silky leather felt fur denim velvet corduroy lace what is it made of

items.html: gossypium, gossypiī n. — cotton (M-O; Plin. NH 19.14 fruticem, quem aliquī gossypion vocant, plūrēs xylon); gossypinus, gossypina, gossypinum — of cotton (M-O, citing Pliny); Pliny’s cotton cloth is xylina. Traupman has no word for cotton.
līnum, līnī n.; linteum, linteī n. — linen; līneus, līnea, līneum — linen, of linen (Traupman 117; M-O).
lāna, lānae f.; lāneus, lānea, lāneum; lānātus — wool; woollen (Traupman 118; M-O). Comenius: Ovibus dētondētur lāna, ex quā cōnficiuntur variae vestēs (Orbis pictus 46).
sēricum, sēricī n.; sēricus, sērica, sēricum — silk; silken (Traupman 118; M-O).
corium, coriī n. — leather; scorteus, scortea, scorteum — leather, of leather (Traupman 117; M-O); M-O also coriaceus (late).
coāctilia, coāctilium n. — felt (M-O; Dig.); pellis, pellis f.; pellicius — fur, of fur (M-O; Traupman 116 amiculum pellicium).
pannus, pannī m.; textum, textī n. — cloth, fabric (Traupman 116; M-O). Velvet, corduroy and lace have only medieval and modern words in M-O (vellūtum, opus denticulātum).
Ex quō facta est haec tunicula? — Ex gossypiō. — What is this T-shirt made of? — Cotton.
Thōrāx lāneus ex lānā ovium fit. — A jumper is made from sheep’s wool.

blocks.html: gossypium and gossypinus are not headwords in the local L&S; Pliny writes the Greek form gossypion (NH 19.14). sēricum: L&S marks the first syllable long (Sēres).

items.html: acus, acūs f. — needle, pin (Traupman 350, 360; Cic.); fīlum, fīlī n. — thread (Traupman 393). Comenius: Sartor discindit pannum forfice, cōnsuitque acū et fīlō duplicātō (Orbis pictus 61).
suō, suere, suī, sūtum — sew (Traupman 377); assuō, assuere — sew on (Hor. AP 16, in L&S: purpureus adsuitur pannus); cōnsuō — sew together.
sarciō, sarcīre, sarsī, sartum — mend (Traupman 345; Cic.).
scindō, scindere, scidī, scissum — tear; scindī — get torn (Traupman 391).
digitāle, digitālis n. — thimble (Traupman 393; not a noun in L&S).
forfex, forficis f. — scissors (Traupman 374; see the shears entry).
fībula, fībulae f. — safety pin (Traupman 117, 373; classically a clasp or brooch); M-O acus innoxia.
acū texere — knit (M-O, after Menge); acū pingere — embroider (M-O; Verg. A. 9.582; Ov.); acū pictus — embroidered.
māchina sūtōria — sewing machine (Traupman 377; Helfer per M-O).
Globulus dēcidit; acū et fīlō rūrsus assuam. — The button’s come off; I’ll sew it back on with a needle and thread.
Brācae tuae scissae sunt; mamma eās sarciet. — Your trousers are torn; Mum will mend them.
Cavē acum; pungit. — Careful with the needle; it pricks.
For washing, drying, folding and ironing, see the laundry entry.
